analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel economy standards for cars, cuts appliance standby power waste, and requires electric utilities to supply rising amounts of renewable energy.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2006 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to five House committees and died in subcommittee without ever reaching a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised fuel economy requirements for new cars and light trucks in steps up to 45 miles per gallon, limited the electricity that appliances waste while switched off, created a national requirement for electric suppliers to get a growing share of power from renewable sources, expanded weatherization help for low-income homes, and made it easier for homeowners with rooftop solar to sell power back to the grid. It also created federal loan guarantees for renewable and clean-coal projects, tax credits for transmission lines and telecommuting, and new energy research programs. It never got past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers would benefit through lower fuel and electricity bills: stricter mileage standards for new cars, limits on standby power drain from household appliances, a national tire efficiency program with labels so buyers could compare, expanded weatherization assistance, and guaranteed net metering so homeowners with small solar or wind systems get credit for power they send to the grid [S2] [S3]. Renewable energy developers and clean-coal projects would gain access to up to $49 billion in federal loan guarantees, extended renewable tax credits, and a federal renewable electricity mandate that creates a market for their power [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, homeowners with solar, renewable developers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the passenger car fuel economy standard in steps from 30 mpg by model year 2012 to 45 mpg after 2016, and extends fuel economy rules to cover much heavier vehicles that were previously excluded
Caps standby power draw of household appliances at 1 watt within three years and sets standards for furnace and air conditioner fan efficiency

Creates a federal renewable portfolio standard requiring retail electric suppliers to reach 20% renewable generation by 2017 and 25% by 2020, with a credit trading system and a cost cap to limit compliance prices
Requires every electric utility to offer net metering so customers with rooftop solar, wind, or fuel cells are credited for excess power they feed back to the grid
Increases and extends weatherization assistance for low-income households and authorizes transit grants for bike paths and pedestrian walkways in transit-oriented development corridors

Cuts nondefense federal government electricity use by 35% by 2015, requires LEED silver green building standards for new federal buildings, and requires agencies to buy hybrid or high-efficiency vehicles
Authorizes up to $49 billion in loan guarantees for biorefineries, wind, solar, geothermal, ocean energy, biomass, and coal plants that capture 90% of their carbon emissions

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of meeting much stricter mileage standards, including higher civil penalties for violations, and electric utilities would bear the cost of buying renewable power or credits, costs they could recover through rates [S3]. The federal government would take on the cost of the loan guarantee program, new research funding, and Energy Star program funding, and taxpayers bear residual risk if guaranteed projects fail [S3].

drawbacks.text: The $49 billion loan guarantee program puts taxpayers on the hook if borrowers default, and the bill authorizes guarantees for coal plants so long as they sequester 90% of carbon emissions, directing federal support to a technology with an uncertain track record

Stricter fuel economy and appliance standards raise upfront costs for manufacturers that would be passed into vehicle and appliance prices, and the bill allows the Energy Secretary to grant exemptions where savings would not offset price increases
The renewable portfolio standard lets utilities recover their full incremental compliance costs from rate-regulated customers, meaning much of the mandate's cost would flow to electricity bills

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-side benefits are real and direct: higher mileage standards, lower standby power waste, tire efficiency labels, weatherization, and net metering all put money back in household budgets over time. The main costs fall on manufacturers and utilities, much of which would be passed to consumers, and the large loan guarantee program carries genuine taxpayer risk, including for coal projects. On balance the bill is a substantial consumer and environmental measure, though its scale and the credit-trading design left plenty of room for compliance to be cheaper than the mandate intended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2006, split among five House committees and several subcommittees, and never came out of any of them before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Cardin introduced the American Energy Independence Act on July 27, 2006, in the final months of the 109th Congress

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Government Reform, and Science committees, and within days was further referred to subcommittees on highways, energy and air quality, environment, energy, and research
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, no markup or floor action is recorded, and it received no cosponsors
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died with it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and electric utilities were better off because the bill never moved: the stricter mileage standards, standby power limits, and renewable electricity mandate never took effect, and the status quo on federal energy policy continued unchanged for the remainder of the Congress.

for.name: Rep. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to five committees; no other members cosponsored it

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality on August 1, 2006; no markup or report followed

against.name: House Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Government Reform, and Science Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral; none ever reported it back for floor consideration

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan breakdown can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill raises mileage standards to 45 mpg and extends coverage to much heavier vehicles, plus it more than doubles civil penalties for violations. Automakers avoided all of this when the bill died.

A federal renewable mandate of 25% by 2020 and required net metering would force changes, but the bill lets utilities recover full compliance costs from ratepayers and gives them a credit cost cap of 3 cents per kilowatt-hour.

The bill locks renewables into the power system through a federal mandate, creates a tradeable credit market, extends production tax credits through 2017, and offers up to $49 billion in loan guarantees for new facilities.

Up to $7 billion in loan guarantees for coal plants that sequester 90% of their carbon dioxide gives the coal industry a federal backstop for a cleaner-fossil pathway, though taxpayers share the default risk.
A 1-watt standby power limit and new fan efficiency standards raise compliance costs, but the bill includes an exemption process where consumer savings would not cover price increases.
A national tire efficiency program would require testing, labeling, minimum fuel economy standards, and retailer disclosures, which improves the information buyers get but adds compliance work.
Steeply higher fuel economy standards and a federal push toward renewable electricity and efficiency would cut gasoline and power demand over time; the industry lost nothing because the bill died.
